documents.content:
# FixRouteBench card

## Summary

FixRouteBench 0.1 is a 50-case deterministic benchmark for civic responsibility routing. It uses fictional jurisdictions and providers so it can be distributed and replayed without presenting stale contact guidance.

## Composition

- 50 episodes
- 10 hard-case families
- 2 adjacent fictional municipalities
- 1 fictional regional road provider
- 3 main issue classes
- Resolved and open-set outcomes

## Episode fields

Each JSONL row includes the observation, event time, decision time, hypotheses, initially visible evidence, action-revealed evidence, costs, latency, duplicate candidates, corrected target, minimum sufficient evidence, escalation path, and historical-label limitation.

## Intended metrics

- Provider accuracy
- Service-code accuracy
- Joint provider and service accuracy
- Wrong-jurisdiction rate
- Duplicate accuracy
- Selective coverage
- Abstention accuracy
- Confidence summaries
- Search cost and latency

## Non-claims

The benchmark does not estimate real-world accuracy, fairness, resident outcomes, resolution time, or final resolution rate. The generated cases are contract tests and feasibility scaffolding.

## Expansion protocol

A 500-case release should use two annotators and one adjudicator, retain source spans, track disagreement, compute agreement by field, preserve decision-time snapshots, and separate expert gold from historical weak labels.

documents.title: whofixesthis — docs/data_governance.md
documents.content:
# Data governance

## Data classes

| Class | Examples | Default handling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Public metadata | Service definitions and public boundaries | Frozen with provenance |
| User observation | Description and observation time | Session scoped |
| Precise location | GPS point and uncertainty | Minimize and allow coarsening |
| User media | Issue photo and close-up | Local browser session only |
| Derived decision | Hypotheses, evidence, confidence | Export only after review |
| Sensitive infrastructure | Utility topology and protected assets | Do not expose |

## Collection principles

- Collect only what can change the route
- Keep uncertainty rather than inventing precision
- Do not infer identity, blame, liability, or entitlement
- Separate media analysis from provider responsibility
- Preserve original public records alongside normalized records
- Retain contradictions

## Retention

The public demo has no server-side user data store. Browser media references and form state disappear with the session. A local prepared report is created only after the user checks the review box and presses export.

Future deployments with persistence must define a retention window, deletion path, export path, encryption policy, access audit, and incident process before collecting user data.

## Provenance

Each evidence item carries a source identifier, authority, canonical URL, retrieval timestamp, checksum, evidence span, valid-time interval, and transaction-time interval.

## Governance review gates

- Source redistribution rights
- Historical label validity
- Geographic and demographic coverage gaps
- Sensitive infrastructure exposure
- Media redaction quality
- Provider dispute and correction process
- Approval enforcement
- Prospective outcome access

documents.title: whofixesthis — docs/model_card.md
documents.content:
# Model card

## Model details

WhoFixesThis 0.1 uses a deterministic evidence-scoring resolver. The default release does not call a language, vision, embedding, or external model.

## Intended use

- Research on temporal civic service routing
- Testing bitemporal graph and provenance contracts
- Studying calibrated abstention and evidence acquisition
- Demonstrating approval-gated local report preparation

## Out of scope

- Legal responsibility findings
- Enforcement, blame, or entitlement decisions
- Emergency dispatch
- Autonomous government submission
- Public utility topology discovery
- Real-world performance claims from fictional fixtures

## Inputs

Description, latitude, longitude, location uncertainty, observation time, optional context identifier, optional asset identifier, and optional local image references.

## Outputs

A provider-service hypothesis list, selected route or unresolved state, confidence, supporting and contradicting evidence, duplicates, next action, escalation path, and counterfactual.

## Decision rule

Evidence scores are filtered by event time and decision time. The top hypothesis must pass a confidence threshold and a margin over the runner-up. Broader GPS uncertainty lowers all candidate scores.

## Limitations

The deterministic keyword and fixture logic is not a trained model. Confidence values are engineering scores for testing selective decision paths. They are not calibrated against expert civic routing outcomes.

## Evaluation

FixRouteBench verifies internal contracts and expected behavior on fictional cases. A publishable empirical result requires independently corrected cases, pre-registered metrics, geographic splits, uncertainty intervals, and leakage controls.

documents.title: freshindex — README.md
documents.content:
# FreshIndex

FreshIndex schedules proactive verification for mutable agent memory when audit capacity is limited. It assigns each memory an age-aware priority, explains the score, dispatches only allowlisted verifiers, and records every decision in a tamper-evident event log.

[Live dashboard](https://pxnkit.github.io/freshindex/) | [API reference](http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs) | [Research scope](docs/research_scope.md)

The repository is a working research prototype. It includes a FastAPI service, a deterministic simulator, conservative posterior policies, exact small-state validation, symbolic checks, a React dashboard, paper artifacts, and automated tests.

## Why this exists

Long-running agents store facts that can change outside the agent. Verification reduces the risk of using stale memory, but checking every item on every round is rarely practical. A useful scheduler has to decide which few items deserve attention now.

FreshIndex models an item's verification age as the state of a restless arm. For the base model, the stale probability after age \(a\) is

\[
q(a) = 1 - (1 - h)^a
\]

where \(h\) is the per-period change hazard. If the item is used with probability \(\lambda\) and a stale use incurs loss \(L\), its expected one-period stale-use cost is

\[
c(a) = \lambda L q(a)
\]

The renewal comparison between auditing at age \(a\) and waiting one more period gives the break-even activation charge

\[
W(a) = (a + 1)c(a + 1) - \sum_{s=0}^{a} c(s)
\]

For nondecreasing \(c(a)\), adjacent scores satisfy

\[
W(a + 1) - W(a) = (a + 2)[c(a + 2) - c(a + 1)] \ge 0
\]

This monotonicity gives the single-item threshold and indexability result under the assumptions stated in [the theorem ledger](theory/theorem_status.md). Item-specific verification cost is subtracted from \(W(a)\). The production scheduler selects up to the available capacity from positive adjusted scores.

The hard-capacity multi-item policy is not presented as a general optimal solution to the coupled restless bandit problem. The proof covers the decoupled Lagrangian relaxation. The ranked policy is a transparent projection back to a per-round capacity limit.

## What is implemented

- Closed-form known-parameter index with stable boundary handling
- Posterior mean, Thompson, and conservative upper-bound policies
- Fixed TTL, oldest-first, immediate-risk, and deterministic random baselines
- Beta approximation for interval-censored geometric hazard feedback
- Gamma-Poisson usage-rate learning
- Forced exploration and fairness credits
- Exact finite-horizon dynamic programming for small validation instances
- Deterministic synthetic worlds with shocks and audit false negatives
- FastAPI endpoints for memory ingestion, scheduling, audit lifecycle, replay, comparison, and export
- Typed verifier adapters with an explicit allowlist
- Canonical evidence hashes and HMAC signatures
- Append-only hash-chained events
- Browser dashboard with a local API mode and a static deterministic demo mode
- Symbolic, unit, property, API, concurrency, integration, and UI tests

## Quick start

FreshIndex requires Python 3.11 or newer and Node.js 20 or newer.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
```

On Windows:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -e ".[dev,analytics]"
.\.venv\Scripts\freshindex verify-proofs
.\.venv\Scripts\freshindex simulate --config configs/smoke.yaml
.\.venv\Scripts\freshindex serve
```

On macOS or Linux:

```bash
./.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ".[dev,analytics]"
./.venv/bin/freshindex verify-proofs
./.venv/bin/freshindex simulate --config configs/smoke.yaml
./.venv/bin/freshindex serve
```

The API starts at `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. Its OpenAPI documentation is available at `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`.

Start the dashboard in another terminal:

```bash
cd ui
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5173`. The dashboard connects to the local API automatically. When no API is available, it uses a deterministic in-browser fleet so the public static deployment remains interactive.

## CLI

Run a configured simulation:

```bash
freshindex simulate --config configs/smoke.yaml --output runs/smoke
```

Preview a schedule from a JSON state:

```bash
freshindex schedule --state examples/state.json --budget 2 --policy conservative
```

Inspect a saved run:

```bash
freshindex replay --manifest runs/smoke/manifest.json
```

Run the symbolic identities:

```bash
freshindex verify-proofs
```

Start the service:

```bash
freshindex serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
```

## API workflow

The normal audit lifecycle has four steps.

1. Register or ingest a memory with `POST /v1/items`
2. Preview capacity allocation with `POST /v1/schedule/preview`
3. Dispatch an allowlisted verifier with `POST /v1/audits/dispatch`
4. Record a signed result with `POST /v1/audits/complete`

The demo verifier can be executed synchronously:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/audits/dispatch \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"item_id":"ITEM_UUID","deadline_seconds":60,"execute":true}'
```

Fresh and stale outcomes reset age. A stale outcome also creates a new memory version. Inconclusive and error outcomes remain in the evidence log but do not reset age. A second concurrent audit for the same memory is rejected.

Useful read endpoints:

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /health` | Service and event-chain health |
| `GET /v1/items` | Fleet state and current beliefs |
| `GET /v1/events` | Ordered append-only events |
| `GET /v1/replay` | State rebuilt from the event stream |
| `GET /v1/export` | Portable research snapshot |
| `POST /v1/policies/compare` | Counterfactual schedules on one state |

## Scheduler conventions

FreshIndex uses an activation-charge convention. The base index is the total charge at which auditing now and waiting one more age step have equal renewal cost. If an item has audit cost \(v_i\), its selection priority is

\[
I_i(a) = W_i(a) - v_i
\]

A round selects at most \(B\) items with positive priority. Exact ties are ordered by age and stable item identifier. The full tie groups remain in `ScheduleDecision`, which makes replay independent of process ordering.

Boundary behavior is intentional:

- \(h = 0\), \(\lambda = 0\), or \(L = 0\) gives a zero index
- \(h = 1\) is handled without numerical cancellation
- \(B = 0\) selects nothing
- \(B \ge N\) still skips nonpositive adjusted scores because capacity is an upper bound
- Empty and fully retired fleets return an empty schedule
- Ages saturate at the configured cap
- At the cap, cost is treated as saturated and the score compares auditing with remaining at the cap

## Learning policy

Verification at age \(a\) reveals whether at least one change occurred, not the exact change time. This feedback is interval-censored. The current hazard learner uses a conservative Beta approximation:

- A fresh outcome contributes \(a\) observed no-change periods
- A stale outcome contributes one change and no assumed pre-change exposure
- The conservative policy ranks with upper uncertainty bounds
- Thompson policy samples from the current approximate posterior

This update is labeled `EMPIRICAL_ONLY` in the theorem ledger. It is not a conjugate posterior for censored change time and no regret theorem is claimed. The benchmark package tests its calibration and failure modes.

Usage uses a Gamma-Poisson exposure model. Loss is supplied by the application and may be paired with external uncertainty analysis. A production deployment should connect loss values to a governed risk taxonomy.

## Verification safety

Verifiers are registered as typed adapters. A request can select an adapter by name, but it cannot provide code, an import path, or a shell command. Every accepted result must satisfy all of these checks:

- The action exists and is still current
- The action and result refer to the same memory
- The evidence hash matches canonical JSON
- The signature matches the adapter secret
- Status-specific fields are present
- No completed action is accepted twice

The bundled HMAC signer is suitable for a local prototype. A production system should use an external key manager and asymmetric signatures so verifiers do not share signing material with the scheduler.

## Reproducibility

Simulation randomness is split into deterministic world and policy streams. A run manifest stores the configuration, seed, metric table, and event trace. Decision records contain every score, selected item, tie group, policy version, seed, and state digest.

Run the full validation suite:

```bash
pytest
ruff check .
mypy freshindex
cd ui
npm test
npm run build
```

The continuous integration workflow runs the same checks on Python 3.11 and 3.12. It also compares formula behavior with renewal calculations and exact small-state dynamic programming.

Research artifacts are organized as follows:

```text
theory/
  proofs/                Human-readable proofs
  theorem_status.md      Claim and proof-status ledger
  notation.md            Symbols and conventions
  counterexamples.md     Known failures outside the base model
paper/
  claims/                Claims and evidence mapping
  results/               Machine-readable experiment summaries
  related_work.bib       Scholarly references
  reproducibility.md     Artifact checklist
configs/
  smoke.yaml             Deterministic acceptance run
  sources.yaml           Source and license registry
```

## Research status

The base single-item threshold and indexability claims are proved for nondecreasing age cost with perfect, immediate reset. Symbolic identities and exhaustive numerical checks back the derivation. They do not replace the stated proof.

The following features are empirical:

- Unknown hazard learning from censored outcomes
- Conservative uncertainty bonuses
- Hard-capacity multi-item ranking
- Imperfect audits
- Delayed results
- Correlated changes
- Abrupt hazard shifts

Results from these tracks must be described as measurements. The project does not call an empirical pattern a proof.

## Source and attribution policy

This repository contains original code, prose, tests, and figures. It does not contain third-party paper files or copied research implementations. Established concepts are cited in the source registry and paper bibliography. Citation is used to separate prior work from this prototype's contribution, not to claim another author's work.

See [docs/source_registry.md](docs/source_registry.md) for versions, licenses, intended use, and checksums. See [paper/claims/evidence.md](paper/claims/evidence.md) for the claim boundary.

## Limitations

FreshIndex is not a compliance engine and does not decide whether evidence is legally sufficient. It assumes that age is a useful state summary and that per-item hazard, usage, and loss can be estimated. Correlation, observation delay, adversarial changes, and verifier bias can invalidate the ranking. The simulator includes these stressors so failures are visible.

The static dashboard is a client-side demonstration. It does not persist data or execute the Python verifier service. Run the FastAPI application for signed audit lifecycle, event replay, and API integration.

## License

MIT License. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

documents.title: freshindex — docs/architecture.md
documents.content:
# Architecture

FreshIndex separates decision logic from verification execution.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Memory and use events"] --> B["Validated domain contracts"]
    B --> C["Append-only event store"]
    B --> D["Hazard and usage beliefs"]
    D --> E["Index and baseline policies"]
    E --> F["Capacity scheduler"]
    F --> G["Audit actions"]
    G --> H["Allowlisted verifier adapters"]
    H --> I["Signed evidence"]
    I --> B
    C --> J["Deterministic replay"]
    E --> K["Simulator and exact oracle"]
    F --> L["FastAPI and React dashboard"]
```

## Components

`freshindex/domain` contains the contracts accepted across API, storage, and verifier boundaries.

`freshindex/theory` contains the analytical score, renewal calculations, symbolic identities, and the exact small-instance dynamic program.

`freshindex/learning` contains the interval-censored hazard approximation and usage-rate posterior.

`freshindex/scheduler` produces a complete `ScheduleDecision`, including unselected scores and tie groups.

`freshindex/verification` contains the allowlist and evidence authentication helpers.

`freshindex/persistence` provides a hash-chained JSONL event log. DuckDB is an optional analytics dependency, not a command execution surface.

`freshindex/simulator` runs deterministic synthetic worlds and writes portable manifests.

`freshindex/api` exposes the application service. The React application uses the API locally and a deterministic in-browser model on static hosting.

## Trust boundaries

The API validates every external payload. The scheduler never imports a verifier named by a request. Evidence is canonicalized before hashing. Completion checks action identity, in-flight ownership, evidence hash, signature, and idempotency.

The current event store serializes appends with a process lock. Production deployment requires a transactional database or durable log with cross-process concurrency control.

documents.title: freshindex — docs/research_scope.md
documents.content:
# Research scope

## Research question

Can a transparent age-based audit index reduce stale-use loss under limited verification capacity, relative to fixed TTL and immediate-risk scheduling, without hiding model failure?

## Base model

The proof package assumes:

- Independent memory items
- Discrete rounds
- Observable verification age
- Constant per-period geometric change hazard
- Independent usage
- Fixed stale-use loss
- Perfect audit
- Immediate reset
- Nondecreasing age cost
- Average-cost objective

These assumptions produce a renewal cycle and a closed-form break-even audit charge.

## System contribution

FreshIndex connects the analytical score to an auditable service. It records the parameters used for each decision, exposes score decomposition, isolates verifiers behind typed adapters, distinguishes all audit outcomes, and supports deterministic replay.

## Novelty boundary

The project does not claim to invent restless bandits, Whittle indices, posterior sampling, or agent memory. Its contribution is the specified age-cost model, the implementation discipline around proactive memory verification, and the linked theory-to-test artifact.

The hard-capacity ranking policy and conservative censored-feedback learner are evaluated algorithms. They are not covered by the base theorem.

## Falsification criteria

The research claim should be narrowed or withdrawn if any of these preregistered checks fail:

- The formula disagrees with adjacent renewal-cost indifference
- The index decreases under a cost sequence that satisfies the base assumptions
- Immediate-risk scheduling matches the index policy across the preregistered heterogeneous sweep
- Proactive verification has negligible value under realistic audit cost
- Real tracks violate the age-state ordering strongly enough that the score is not interpretable
- Learned hazard intervals show material and persistent miscalibration

documents.title: hippogate — README.md
documents.content:
# HippoGate

HippoGate is a research system for deciding what an adaptive agent should do with a candidate memory. It can forget the candidate, keep it episodically, run a targeted cross-context probe, or consolidate it into semantic memory.

The controller treats cross-context applicability as a hidden binary state. It maintains a calibrated posterior belief and solves a discounted belief-state decision problem. This makes the consolidation rule inspectable. Every decision can be traced to the posterior, cost model, horizon, recurrence estimate, and probe likelihoods that produced it.

The repository includes the mathematical core, finite and infinite-horizon solvers, direct enumeration checks, synthetic and procedural environments, baseline policies, an API, a command-line interface, and an interactive phase diagram.

Live phase diagram: [pxnkit.github.io/hippogate](https://pxnkit.github.io/hippogate/)

## Why this project exists

Memory systems often use rules such as "store after two successful uses" or "keep anything above a confidence threshold." Those rules ignore the cost of a wrong generalization, the value of another observation, the probability that a memory will recur, and the quality of the available validation context.

HippoGate asks a narrower and testable question:

> Given current evidence and explicit costs, which memory action has the highest expected value?

This framing is useful when an experience may be valid in one context but unsafe in another. Examples include retry procedures, schema mappings, tool-use workflows, API conventions, and learned task strategies.

HippoGate does not update model weights in its default path. Consolidation creates an explicit, versioned semantic rule with scope, evidence, posterior, validation contexts, provenance, and rollback metadata. Parameter updates can be added as a separate adapter without changing the core decision problem.

## Decision model

For one candidate rule, let the hidden applicability state be

```text
z = 0  context-specific
z = 1  reusable
```

The controller never observes `z`. It maintains

```text
p_t = P(z = 1 | evidence through time t)
```

A probe produces an outcome under a context-dependent likelihood model. For an observed outcome `y`, the exact Bayesian update is

```text
       p P(y | z = 1)
p' = -------------------------------
     p P(y | z = 1) + (1-p) P(y | z = 0)
```

The implementation evaluates four actions:

| Action | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `forget` | Stop tracking the candidate and accept possible missed value |
| `episodic` | Keep the candidate without generalizing it and pay a retention cost |
| `probe` | Validate the candidate in another context and update the posterior |
| `consolidate` | Store a scoped semantic rule and accept possible interference |

Terminal values are linear in the belief. Probe and episodic values include discounted continuation value. The solver computes the Bellman maximum over every available action.

The default reward model exposes:

- reusable semantic value
- harmful interference cost
- consolidation cost
- missed useful consolidation cost
- episodic storage cost
- recurrence probability
- probe cost
- discount

No cost is hidden inside a learned score.

## What is implemented

### Mathematical core

- log-odds Bayesian updates with exact handling for priors at zero and one
- missing evidence support
- explicit failure for observations that are impossible under both states
- context-specific multi-outcome likelihood models
- finite-horizon belief-grid dynamic programming
- infinite-horizon value iteration with residual and error-bound reporting
- direct belief-tree enumeration for small problems
- adaptive grid points near analytical terminal crossings
- action-region and threshold extraction
- coarse-to-fine value and policy stability checks
- entropy-based probe scoring
- Blackwell garbling checks for controlled probe pairs

### Memory and evaluation

- typed candidate experiences and proposed semantic rules
- strict separation of hidden simulator state from controller-visible state
- explicit evidence history
- versioned semantic memory entries
- interference recording and thresholded rollback
- deterministic rule extraction for reproducible fixtures
- synthetic reusable and context-specific rule streams
- procedural API and tool-use task families
- fixed-success, fixed-confidence, recency, uncertainty, random replay, and terminal baselines
- paired-seed benchmark execution
- bootstrap confidence intervals
- harmful consolidation and missed consolidation metrics
- deterministic run manifests with source and configuration hashes

### Application surfaces

- FastAPI service with OpenAPI documentation
- CLI for solving, simulation, benchmarking, verification, and reproduction
- React and TypeScript phase diagram
- local browser-side solver for static deployment
- downloadable configuration and results
- Docker images for the API and phase diagram
- GitHub Actions for Python, web, and Pages deployment

## Repository layout

```text
hippogate/
  src/hippogate/
    api/
    belief/
    environments/
    evaluation/
    extraction/
    mdp/
    memory/
    policies/
    probes/
    reporting/
    solvers/
  apps/web/
  theory/
  configs/
  data/fixtures/
  tests/
  paper/
  artifacts/
```

The Python package is the reference implementation. The browser solver implements the same single-probe finite-horizon recurrence for the public phase diagram. Cross-language regression tests protect their shared default regime.

## Quick start

HippoGate requires Python 3.12.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

On Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

Solve the default two-threshold configuration:

```bash
hippogate solve configs/synthetic/two_threshold.yaml
```

Simulate one candidate:

```bash
hippogate simulate configs/benchmark/smoke.yaml --seed 17
```

Run a paired-seed benchmark:

```bash
hippogate benchmark configs/benchmark/smoke.yaml --episodes 500
```

Verify a recorded run:

```bash
hippogate verify-policy <run-id>
```

Reproduce a recorded benchmark:

```bash
hippogate reproduce <run-id>
```

Start the API:

```bash
hippogate serve
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` for the generated API documentation.

## Run the phase diagram

The web application requires Node.js 22 and pnpm.

```bash
cd apps/web
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm dev
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:5173`.

The phase diagram runs locally in the browser. It does not send candidate data to the API. Change the prior, recurrence, interference cost, episodic cost, probe cost, probe accuracy, discount, and horizon to inspect how the optimal action regions move.

The candidate trajectory panel applies successful or failed cross-context observations one at a time. The comparison panel shows how the posterior policy differs from fixed-success rules.

## Docker

Run the API and static phase diagram together:

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

The API is available at `http://127.0.0.1:8000`.

The phase diagram is available at `http://127.0.0.1:4173`.

## API example

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/solve \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "prior": 0.5,
    "horizon": 6,
    "discount": 0.95,
    "recurrence": 0.85,
    "grid_size": 801
  }'
```

The response includes the belief grid, optimal values, policy labels, contiguous action regions, and a coarse-to-fine stability report.

## Reproducibility contract

Every benchmark run records:

- full solver configuration
- paired seeds
- grid size
- solver tolerance
- environment identifier
- source tree hash
- configuration hash
- raw policy summary

Run directories are intentionally excluded from version control. Paper-linked artifacts are generated into `artifacts/generated` and promoted to `artifacts/reference` only after review.

The repository does not contain invented benchmark tables. Any committed empirical artifact must be generated by a repository command and include its manifest.

## Numerical accuracy

The finite-horizon solver is exact on its disclosed belief grid. It uses linear interpolation for posterior continuation points that fall between grid nodes. It does not claim an exact continuous-belief solution.

Use `hippogate.solvers.diagnostics.compare_grids` to measure the maximum value difference and action agreement between two grid resolutions. The API returns this report for every finite-horizon solve.

The direct enumerator has no belief-grid interpolation. It is intended for small horizons and test points because its observation tree grows exponentially.

The infinite-horizon solver requires a discount below one. It reports convergence status, the final Bellman residual, and the residual-based sup-norm error bound. Nonconvergence is returned as a result, not hidden.

## Theory and claim status

The `theory` directory separates definitions, assumptions, proof sketches, numerical checks, and counterexamples. Claims use one of five labels:

- `PROVED`
- `PARTIAL`
- `EMPIRICAL`
- `FALSIFIED`
- `UNTESTED`

The current release proves only results whose assumptions and argument are fully stated in the repository. General ordered regions with episodic retention are not assumed. When a parameter choice breaks a clean ordering, the exact dynamic program remains the source of truth.

See [theory/CLAIMS.md](theory/CLAIMS.md) and [theory/ASSUMPTIONS.md](theory/ASSUMPTIONS.md).

## Testing

Run the Python checks:

```bash
ruff check .
mypy src
pytest --cov=hippogate --cov-report=term-missing
```

Run the browser checks:

```bash
cd apps/web
pnpm test
pnpm build
pnpm exec playwright install chromium
pnpm test:e2e
```

The test suite covers posterior boundaries, likelihood normalization, impossible observations, brute-force agreement, Bellman contraction behavior, policy regions, probe informativeness, hidden-state separation, reproducibility hashes, API contracts, seeded simulation, and rollback behavior.

## Research scope

HippoGate is a decision and evaluation framework. It is not evidence that biological memory follows this implementation. It is not a clinical model. It does not make claims about human cognition.

The default benchmark uses synthetic and deterministic procedural tasks. Performance on these tasks does not establish general agent-memory improvements. A serious empirical claim requires held-out task families, frozen configurations, paired seeds, confidence intervals, extraction-error ablations, and evidence that solver discretization is not driving the result.

The kill criteria in [paper/KILL_CRITERIA.md](paper/KILL_CRITERIA.md) define outcomes that should stop or reformulate the project.

## Security and privacy

The default application runs without credentials and stores no user data. The browser phase diagram is entirely local. The API accepts model parameters and synthetic benchmark requests only.

Do not put private prompts, credentials, or production memories into committed fixtures. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for reporting instructions.

## Citation

If you use this software in research, cite the release metadata in [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff). Cite the established decision-theory and memory literature relevant to your own claims separately.

## License

Apache License 2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

documents.content:
# HypothesisOps

HypothesisOps is a research platform for safe, sequential cloud incident diagnosis. It keeps several causal explanations alive, predicts what each explanation implies, and selects a bounded observation or sandbox intervention that can separate them.

The first release proves the complete loop in a deterministic simulator. It includes paired ambiguous incidents, typed actions, a fail-closed safety policy, value-of-information search, baseline policies, replay notebooks, statistical summaries, an HTTP API, a CLI, a small container testbed, and a live investigation workbench.

The system does not connect to production services. It cannot execute model-generated shell commands.

## Project status

| Capability | Status | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deterministic paired incidents | Working | 8 families and 16 episodes |
| Safe typed observations | Working | Allowlist, scope, budget, timeout, and audit checks |
| Active hypothesis search | Working | VoI per cost, uncertainty, runbook, random, and passive policies |
| Replay and integrity checks | Working | Atomic JSON notebook with SHA-256 verification |
| Live investigation workbench | Working | Two interactive cases with export and recovery verification |
| HTTP API and CLI | Working | Session, step, replay, benchmark, and serve commands |
| Container fixture | Implemented | Compose profile included, Docker execution not run in this build environment |
| External cloud benchmark validity | Untested | No external performance claim is made |
| Human on-call impact | Untested | No user study has been run |

## Why active diagnosis

Two incidents can look the same in passive telemetry. A checkout delay caused by database saturation can initially resemble a retry storm. A regional timeout policy can resemble packet loss.

HypothesisOps treats the next observation as a decision:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Ambiguous symptom"] --> B["Competing causal hypotheses"]
    B --> C["Predict probe outcomes"]
    C --> D["Safety and budget gate"]
    D --> E["Run one bounded probe"]
    E --> F["Update belief state"]
    F --> G{"Verified or confident"}
    G -->|No| C
    G -->|Yes| H["Diagnosis, audit, and replay"]
```

The controller scores expected information and decision improvement against telemetry volume, elapsed time, risk, and disruption. Every requested action passes through the safety policy before execution.

## Live workbench

The Incident Investigation Workbench is a complete browser implementation of the research loop. It supports:

- Switching between paired ambiguous incidents
- Inspecting topology, symptoms, and causal chains
- Comparing live hypothesis scores
- Selecting safe probes with predicted gain and cost
- Updating belief state from deterministic observations
- Recording allowed and blocked actions
- Verifying a recovery in a digital twin
- Exporting a replayable JSON notebook
- Reviewing executed smoke benchmark results

The browser demo uses deterministic local fixtures. The Python controller implements the same system boundary for experiments and API use.

## Quick start

### Python controller

Python 3.12 is required.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
hypothesisops diagnose db-vs-retry:b --seed 1847
```

On Windows PowerShell, activate the environment with:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

Start the API:

```bash
hypothesisops serve
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` for the generated API reference.

### Investigation workbench

Node.js 22.13 or newer is required.

```bash
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open the local URL printed by the development server.

### Container profile

```bash
docker compose up --build
```

The API is exposed on `http://127.0.0.1:8000`. The fixture dependency stays on the private Compose network.

## CLI

```text
hypothesisops init
hypothesisops validate-environment configs/environments/local.json
hypothesisops inject db-vs-retry:a
hypothesisops diagnose db-vs-retry:b
hypothesisops replay artifacts/replays/<session-id>.json
hypothesisops benchmark configs/benchmark/smoke.yaml
hypothesisops report artifacts/smoke-benchmark.json
hypothesisops serve
```

The `inject` command creates a simulator episode. It does not mutate a cluster or service.

## API example

Create an investigation:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"case_id":"db-vs-retry:b","seed":1847}'
```

Run the controller-selected next action:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/sessions/<session-id>/steps \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{}'
```

The response contains the full agent-visible episode, current hypotheses, observations, stop state, and audit ledger.

## Deterministic smoke benchmark

The checked-in smoke result is generated from 8 paired families and 16 episodes with seed 2025. These numbers test the software protocol. They are not evidence of performance on a real cloud environment.

| Policy | Top-1 | Mean actions | Mean telemetry | Mean risk |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| VoI per cost | 100% | 1.88 | 18.6 KB | 0.05 |
| Uncertainty only | 100% | 1.63 | 17.1 KB | 0.05 |
| Fixed runbook | 100% | 2.13 | 21.6 KB | 0.06 |
| Random safe | 100% | 1.88 | 19.8 KB | 0.06 |
| Passive abstention | 0% | 0.00 | 0 KB | 0.00 |

The passive baseline abstains because both members of each pair expose the same initial evidence. Active policies receive the same typed action space. A result only counts as diagnosed after the confidence stop rule is reached.

Regenerate the result:

```bash
hypothesisops benchmark configs/benchmark/smoke.yaml \
  --seed 2025 \
  --output artifacts/smoke-benchmark.json
```

The result file includes raw per-episode records, bootstrap intervals, Brier scores, and an integrity hash.

## Safety model

The default policy is intentionally narrow:

- Targets must begin with `sandbox/`, `digital-twin/`, or `snapshot/`
- Action kinds must be typed and allowlisted
- Medium and high risk actions are blocked
- Arbitrary command fields are blocked
- Parent path traversal and Windows path separators are blocked
- Action, telemetry, and risk budgets are enforced
- Repeated actions are blocked
- Every allowed and blocked request produces an audit record

The simulator stores hidden cause metadata in its private session object. The public episode schema has no ground-truth, injector, fault-name, or variant field. Leakage tests scan every public fixture.

See [paper/safety_model.md](paper/safety_model.md) for the threat model and [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for reporting guidance.

## Repository map

```text
app/                         Live investigation workbench
configs/                     Sandbox, action, source, and benchmark manifests
src/hypothesisops/
  api/                       FastAPI service
  benchmark/                 Paired evaluation and leakage audit
  causal/                    Typed causal DAG
  cli/                       Command-line interface
  evidence/                  Compatibility based belief updates
  policies/                  Active and passive selection policies
  safety/                    Fail-closed authorization
  schemas/                   Frozen Pydantic models
  simulation/                Deterministic paired fixtures
  storage/                   Replay integrity and atomic persistence
  testbed/                   Original container fixture
tests/
  api/                       API contract tests
  integration/               Full diagnosis and replay tests
  property/                  Cross-seed invariants
  regression/                Paired ambiguity checks
  safety/                    Adversarial policy tests
  unit/                      Component tests
paper/                       Claims, benchmark, safety, and reproducibility notes
artifacts/                   Executed smoke result
```

## Testing

Run the Python suite:

```bash
pytest --cov=hypothesisops --cov-report=term-missing
```

Run static checks:

```bash
ruff check src tests
mypy src
```

Run the production web build and rendered HTML checks:

```bash
npm test
```

The suite covers deterministic replay, hidden-state separation, topology validity, action budgets, telemetry budgets, risk limits, command injection, namespace escape, path traversal, duplicate actions, public payload leakage, API lifecycle, replay integrity, and paired ambiguity.

## Reproducibility

Each episode records:

- Simulator version and seed
- Immutable topology snapshot hash
- Agent-visible symptom and evidence
- Typed actions and predicted costs
- Raw observations and compatibility values
- Belief updates and stopping reason
- Allowed and blocked action decisions
- Telemetry and risk totals
- Replay integrity hash

The npm dependency graph is locked in `package-lock.json`. Python runtime and development versions are pinned in `pyproject.toml` and `requirements.lock`. The benchmark manifest is stored in `configs/benchmark/smoke.yaml`.

The full reproduction procedure is in [paper/reproducibility.md](paper/reproducibility.md).

## Research boundaries

HypothesisOps is an application and research scaffold. The current evidence supports claims about deterministic fixtures only.

It does not establish:

- Accuracy on an external incident corpus
- Transfer from the simulator to a cloud cluster
- Robustness to model-generated hypotheses
- Safe use against production infrastructure
- Reduced engineer response time
- Improved customer outcomes

The claims registry in [paper/claims.md](paper/claims.md) marks every statement as supported, unsupported, or untested. The project should stop or be reformulated if ambiguity disappears, metadata leaks the cause, safe actions cannot separate a pair, active selection fails to improve the intended cost measure, or the safety boundary cannot block unsafe requests.

## Contributing

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) before opening a change. New incident families must include a paired ambiguity test, a safe discriminating action, a leakage audit, and a deterministic replay.

## Citation

Project citation metadata is available in [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff).

## License

Apache License 2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).

documents.title: methodchain — README.md
documents.content:
# MethodChain

MethodChain reconstructs experimental procedures whose parameters are distributed across cited methods and supporting files.

The system returns a typed protocol, a document search trace, and a parameter lineage graph. Every resolved field points to an exact source span and every unresolved field remains explicit. MethodChain does not turn missing evidence into a plausible recipe.

The default path is deterministic, offline, and based on synthetic CC0 documents. It needs no API key, model endpoint, external database, or restricted publication.

## Current status

MethodChain is a research prototype with a complete vertical slice.

It is suitable for software evaluation, interface research, annotation studies, and extension with legally supplied document collections. It is not validated for laboratory execution and does not provide safety approval.

## What works

- Legal bundle validation with access status, retrieval metadata, SHA-256 hashes, and parser warnings
- Recursive procedural citation discovery with lexical scoring, uncertainty, and abstention
- Typed extraction for materials, substrates, temperatures, gas flows, dwell times, cooling rates, and pressure
- Exact page, section, character span, quote, and document hash provenance
- Main document and supplement merging that preserves conflicting reports
- Strict and permissive parent-child inheritance policies
- Parameter states for reported, inherited, modified, contradicted, and missing evidence
- A queryable lineage graph over documents, protocols, parameters, and evidence
- Target-only, one-hop, breadth-first, budgeted, and oracle traversal policies
- Hard document budget enforcement with a replayable action trace
- Laboratory inventory checks that report supported, incompatible, blocked, and expert-review states
- SQLite run storage and deterministic JSON and Markdown exports
- A FastAPI service and a command-line interface
- An interactive Protocol Lineage Workbench
- A synthetic smoke benchmark with source attribution and unsupported inference checks
- Unit, property, integration, API, scientific regression, adversarial, and web tests
- Docker, Compose, continuous integration, locked dependencies, and a paper package

## Why a lineage graph

A normal extraction pipeline can report a value without explaining how that value survived across method versions.

MethodChain keeps the chain visible.

```text
temperature = 900 C
  reported as 850 C in Ancestor A
  modified to 900 C in Parent B
  explicitly unchanged in Target C

pressure = unresolved
  1.0 bar in Parent B
  0.8 bar in the Parent B supporting record
  contradiction preserved for review
```

The final protocol is a compiled view of the evidence graph. It is not the source of truth.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Legal document bundle] --> B[Manifest and hash validation]
    B --> C[Typed document parsing]
    C --> D[Procedural citation detector]
    D --> E[Budgeted citation search]
    E --> F[Typed protocol extraction]
    F --> G[Parent-child alignment]
    G --> H[Parameter lineage graph]
    H --> I[Inventory compiler]
    H --> J[JSON and human report]
    E --> K[Replayable search trace]
    H --> L[Protocol Lineage Workbench]
```

The default implementation is rule based by design. Optional model adapters can be added behind the same typed contracts without changing provenance requirements.

## Quick start

MethodChain requires Python 3.12.

### Linux, macOS, or WSL

```bash
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
methodchain smoke
```

### PowerShell

```powershell
py -3.12 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
.\.venv\Scripts\methodchain.exe smoke
```

The smoke command reconstructs the bundled chain, compiles it against the example inventory, runs four search policies across four budgets, and writes benchmark artifacts.

## Run the API

```bash
methodchain serve
```

The service starts at `http://127.0.0.1:8000`.

Useful endpoints include:

- `GET /health`
- `GET /api/cases`
- `GET /api/reconstruct/pilot-cvd-chain`
- `POST /api/compile/pilot-cvd-chain`
- `GET /docs`

## Run the workbench

```bash
cd apps/web
npm install
npm run dev
```

The workbench uses the same synthetic chain as the Python smoke path. It lets a reviewer change the document budget, compare traversal policies, select parameters, inspect exact source text, follow lineage events, export JSON, and review local laboratory constraints.

## Command-line interface

```text
methodchain init
methodchain ingest <document-bundle>
methodchain resolve <doi> --enable-network --mailto <address>
methodchain reconstruct --bundle <document-bundle>
methodchain compile --bundle <document-bundle> --inventory <lab.yaml>
methodchain benchmark configs/benchmark/smoke.yaml
methodchain report <run-id>
methodchain serve
methodchain smoke
```

External DOI resolution is disabled unless `--enable-network` is passed. The resolver records metadata only. It does not bypass authentication, retrieve restricted documents, or infer a license.

## Verified offline behavior

The checked smoke run uses one synthetic citation chain with four readable documents.

| Check | Result |
| --- | ---: |
| Readable documents opened | 4 |
| Critical fields with a resolved value | 6 of 7 |
| Source attribution accuracy | 100 percent |
| Contradictions detected | 1 |
| Unsupported inference rate | 0 percent |
| Minimum source set recovered | Yes |
| Inventory result | Incompatible |
| Deterministic benchmark rows | 16 |

These numbers validate the software path on a synthetic fixture. They do not show that MethodChain is scientifically effective on real publications.

## Evidence states

Each parameter carries:

- A normalized value and raw value
- A canonical unit and optional uncertainty
- A source document, page, section, character span, and exact quote
- A document hash
- An evidence state
- Extraction confidence
- Human verification status
- An inheritance claim when the value is inherited
- A lineage path across protocol versions

Strict inheritance accepts a parent value only when the child contains explicit unchanged language. Permissive inheritance also accepts high-confidence procedural references such as `according to` or `adapted from`. Both modes preserve the claim span used to justify the decision.

## Legal access boundary

MethodChain processes only:

- Synthetic fixtures
- User-supplied documents
- Open-access documents
- Licensed documents supplied through an authorized workflow

Known but inaccessible ancestors are recorded as inaccessible. They are never marked as read. Optional metadata adapters for Crossref, OpenAlex, and Unpaywall require explicit configuration.

The repository contains no external paper text, figures, tables, annotations, or reported benchmark results.

## Safety boundary

MethodChain reconstructs evidence. It does not execute experiments.

The inventory compiler checks declared capability such as furnace limits and gas flow. It does not assess chemical hazards, authorize substitutions, validate a risk assessment, or replace expert review.

Every human-readable protocol includes a research-only warning.

## Bundle format

A bundle is a directory with a `bundle.json` manifest and legally supplied document files.

```json
{
  "case_id": "example-chain",
  "title": "Example protocol family",
  "target_document_id": "target",
  "critical_fields": ["temperature", "dwell_time"],
  "documents": [
    {
      "id": "target",
      "work_id": "work-target",
      "title": "Target method",
      "kind": "main",
      "path": "target.txt",
      "license": "User supplied",
      "access_status": "user_supplied",
      "references": [
        {
          "label": "4",
          "target_id": "parent",
          "title": "Parent method"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Document paths must stay inside the bundle root. A bundle is rejected if a readable file is missing, a path escapes the bundle, the target is absent, or a listed supplement cannot be resolved.

## Evaluation

The smoke benchmark compares:

- Target only
- One hop
- Breadth first
- Budgeted gain

It records:

- Critical parameter recall
- Source attribution accuracy
- Contradiction detection
- Unsupported inference rate
- Minimum source set recovery
- Documents opened

The optional benchmark dependency writes Parquet alongside CSV and JSON. The checked repository artifacts remain JSON and CSV so the default path stays lightweight.

Real scientific evaluation requires a preregistered, legally distributable benchmark with protocol-family splits, independent annotation, agreement analysis, and expert review. The current fixture must not be used to support performance claims.

## Development

```bash
ruff check src tests
mypy src/methodchain
pytest --cov=methodchain --cov-report=term-missing
cd apps/web
npm run lint
npm test
```

The test suite checks:

- Legal access and path boundaries
- Citation classification and abstention
- Unit normalization and exact spans
- Strict inheritance invariants
- Contradiction preservation
- Search budget enforcement
- Deterministic replay
- Inventory blocking behavior
- API contracts
- SQLite round trips
- Scientific smoke metrics
- Server-rendered workbench content

## Repository map

```text
methodchain/
  apps/web/                 Protocol Lineage Workbench
  artifacts/                Checked smoke outputs
  configs/                  Domain, search, inventory, and benchmark configs
  data/fixtures/            Synthetic CC0 chain and gold annotations
  docs/                     Architecture and reproducibility notes
  paper/                    Claims, benchmark card, limitations, and paper scaffold
  src/methodchain/
    api/                    FastAPI service
    benchmark/              Metrics and smoke runner
    citations/              Procedural citation detection
    cli/                    Command-line interface
    documents/              Bundle loading and optional adapters
    extraction/             Typed rule extraction
    inventory/              Laboratory constraint compiler
    lineage/                Graph construction and validation
    protocols/              Parent-child alignment
    reporting/              JSON and Markdown export
    schemas/                Pydantic contracts
    search/                 Traversal policies
    storage/                SQLite run store
    validation/             Cross-layer invariants
  tests/                    Unit through end-to-end tests
```

## Research roadmap

The next credible milestone is a pilot of at least 30 legally redistributable chains across two protocol families.

That milestone should include:

1. Double annotation of procedural citations and critical fields
2. Ancestor-family split generation
3. Table and caption extraction
4. OCR failure labels
5. Paired budget curves with confidence intervals
6. Expert correction-time measurement
7. A preregistered unsupported inference threshold

The full benchmark target of 300 to 500 chains should proceed only if the pilot passes the kill criteria in [paper/limitations.md](paper/limitations.md).

## Citation

Citation metadata is available in [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff).

## License

The source code is licensed under Apache-2.0.

The bundled synthetic fixture is released under CC0-1.0.

documents.title: methodchain — docs/architecture.md
documents.content:
# Architecture

MethodChain is organized around evidence-preserving transformations.

## Core data flow

1. A bundle loader validates access state and local paths
2. A parser converts readable files into typed document records
3. A citation detector classifies procedural inheritance claims
4. A search policy chooses the next legal document under a hard budget
5. An extractor creates direct protocol fields with exact spans
6. A work merger combines main text and inspected supplements
7. An aligner classifies parent-child parameter changes
8. A lineage builder connects final fields to all supporting evidence
9. Validators reject unsupported values and graph cycles
10. The inventory compiler checks declared local capability
11. Reporters write replayable JSON and a review-oriented human protocol

## Evidence is immutable

The pipeline does not edit a source record after hashing it. Derived objects reference the source document hash and exact span.

The final protocol is disposable. It can be regenerated from the bundle, configuration, and manifest.

## Inheritance policies

Strict mode requires explicit unchanged language before an unreported child field can inherit a parent value.

Permissive mode also accepts a high-confidence procedural citation. This mode keeps the claim span and remains distinguishable in the run manifest.

Neither mode resolves a contradiction by selecting a value.

## Failure behavior

Parsing warnings remain attached to the document.

Inaccessible ancestors generate a request-user-document action.

Missing fields remain missing.

Duplicate incompatible values become contradictions.

Citation cycles stop reconstruction with an error.

documents.content:
# Threat model

## Protected assets

- User-supplied documents
- Access credentials
- Local file paths
- Run artifacts
- Scientific evidence integrity

## Threats

- Path traversal through a bundle manifest
- Restricted content fetched without authorization
- Prompt or document text treated as executable instruction
- Parser resource exhaustion
- Fabricated parameters accepted without evidence
- Inaccessible documents marked as read
- Contradictions silently collapsed
- Laboratory output mistaken for execution approval

## Controls

- Bundle-root path enforcement
- Disabled network resolvers
- Explicit access states
- Exact source spans and hashes
- Pydantic validation
- Hard document budgets
- Missing and contradicted states
- No laboratory execution tools
- Research-only warnings in reports
- Read-only container configuration

## Remaining risks

The optional PDF parser should run in an isolated resource-limited worker for untrusted uploads.

Future model adapters require prompt-injection testing and output validation against retrieved spans.

documents.title: changepilot — README.md
documents.content:
# ChangePilot

ChangePilot is a version-aware migration workbench for Python projects. It finds API usage that crosses a dependency upgrade boundary, traces the affected local call graph, stages conservative edits, and rejects patches that change code outside the declared rewrite set.

The repository contains two working surfaces:

- An interactive web workbench for exploring the migration flow
- A Python AST engine and command line interface for repository analysis

ChangePilot is an early engineering prototype. It is useful for inspecting a focused upgrade and testing migration contracts. It is not a replacement for a project test suite or a general Python refactoring platform.

## What it does

Given a source tree and a set of current and target dependency versions, ChangePilot performs four steps:

1. It selects API changes whose version boundary is crossed by the upgrade
2. It locates matching call sites with Python AST analysis
3. It follows reverse local calls to estimate the review surface
4. It applies only deterministic edits and verifies a closed patch contract

Rules that need context-sensitive restructuring stay in the review queue. For example, a method rename can be safe enough for an automatic edit while a call shape rewrite remains manual.

## Try the workbench

```bash
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open the local URL printed by the development server. The sample workspace includes Pydantic and NumPy migration findings, a line-level patch preview, and contract verification.

The browser workbench uses a lightweight source detector so it can run without a backend. The Python package is the reference implementation for AST-based analysis.

## Use the Python engine

ChangePilot requires Python 3.11 or newer and has no runtime dependencies.

```bash
python -m venv .venv

# Linux and macOS
source .venv/bin/activate

# Windows PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

python -m pip install -e .
```

Scan the included example:

```bash
changepilot scan examples/release_service.py \
  --from pydantic=1.10.14 \
  --from numpy=1.26.4 \
  --to pydantic=2.7.4 \
  --to numpy=2.0.0
```

Expected output:

```text
Scanned 1 files and 28 lines. Found 3 migration call sites.
examples/release_service.py:12:12 LOW BaseModel.parse_obj -> BaseModel.model_validate
examples/release_service.py:16:12 LOW BaseModel.dict -> BaseModel.model_dump
examples/release_service.py:20:37 LOW numpy.float_ -> numpy.float64
```

Preview the safe patch:

```bash
changepilot migrate examples/release_service.py \
  --from pydantic=1.10.14 \
  --from numpy=1.26.4 \
  --to pydantic=2.7.4 \
  --to numpy=2.0.0
```

Add `--write` only after reviewing the diff.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Current and target versions"] --> B["Version path resolver"]
    C["Python source tree"] --> D["AST index"]
    B --> E["Applicable change rules"]
    D --> F["Call-site matcher"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["Reverse call impact graph"]
    G --> H["Safe patch set"]
    G --> I["Manual review queue"]
    H --> J["Closed patch contract"]
    J --> K["Verified diff"]
```

The core modules have narrow responsibilities:

| Module | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `catalog.py` | Stores API change records and selects rules for a version path |
| `analyzer.py` | Builds AST indexes, matches call sites, and traces reverse callers |
| `migrate.py` | Applies the subset of rules marked as deterministic |
| `evaluation.py` | Verifies patch boundaries and entity state changes |
| `benchmark.py` | Runs labeled positive and negative regression fixtures |
| `cli.py` | Exposes scan, migrate, and benchmark commands |

See [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) for the data contracts and failure boundaries.

## Rule catalog

The starter catalog contains seven rules across Pydantic, NumPy, pandas, and Flask.

| Library | Change | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Pydantic | `BaseModel.dict` to `BaseModel.model_dump` | Automatic |
| Pydantic | `BaseModel.json` to `BaseModel.model_dump_json` | Automatic |
| Pydantic | `BaseModel.parse_obj` to `BaseModel.model_validate` | Automatic |
| NumPy | `numpy.float_` to `numpy.float64` | Automatic |
| NumPy | `numpy.complex_` to `numpy.complex128` | Automatic |
| pandas | `DataFrame.append` to `pandas.concat` | Manual review |
| Flask | Remove the JSON helper `app` keyword | Manual review |

Each rule records a version boundary, match target, replacement, risk level, confidence, edit policy, and upstream documentation URL. A rule is active only when the requested upgrade crosses its boundary.

The catalog is intentionally small. Adding hundreds of weak rules would make the interface look complete while reducing trust in the patch set. See [Rule authoring](docs/rule-authoring.md) for the acceptance checklist.

## Patch contract

Automatic edits are evaluated under a closed patch boundary.

A patch passes when:

- The migrated source parses as Python
- All automatically fixable findings are cleared
- Every changed line maps to an automatic rule
- Lines with manual findings remain unchanged

The state evaluator also supports added, deleted, and updated entity assertions. Any state change that is not explained by an assertion causes verification to fail.

This outcome-based check is useful for testing migration runners and agent workflows. It does not execute untrusted source code.

## Evaluation

Run the regression benchmark:

```bash
changepilot benchmark --output results/baseline.json
```

The checked-in baseline covers 11 labeled fixtures:

- Five exact automatic patch cases
- Two manual review cases
- Four negative or boundary cases

The current fixture result is:

| Metric | Result |
|---|---:|
| Detection precision | 1.0000 |
| Detection recall | 1.0000 |
| Detection F1 | 1.0000 |
| Exact patch rate | 1.0000 |
| Contract pass rate | 1.0000 |

These values describe only the small repository fixture set. They are regression signals, not evidence of broad performance on arbitrary projects.

## Test suite

```bash
# Python unit and contract tests
python -m unittest discover -s python/tests -v

# Python lint and formatting checks
python -m ruff check python/src python/tests examples
python -m ruff format --check python/src python/tests examples

# Web build and rendered output tests
npm test

# TypeScript and React lint
npm run lint
```

The Python suite currently contains 25 tests covering:

- Version boundary selection
- Import alias resolution
- Typed Pydantic receiver detection
- NumPy namespace changes
- pandas review routing
- Reverse caller tracing
- Syntax error handling
- Safe rewrite idempotence
- Closed patch rejection
- Entity state diff assertions
- Benchmark metric generation

GitHub Actions runs the Python and web suites independently.

## Repository layout

```text
app/                         Interactive workbench
src/engine/                  Browser analysis model
python/src/changepilot/      Python AST engine and CLI
python/tests/                Unit and contract tests
examples/                    Small original migration example
results/baseline.json        Reproducible fixture benchmark output
docs/                        Architecture and rule authoring notes
.github/workflows/           Continuous integration
```

## Design decisions

### Deterministic before generative

The first release does not call an LLM. Every automatic edit must be explainable by a catalog rule and testable with an exact contract. A future model-backed planner can propose candidates, but it should not weaken the verification boundary.

### Version paths are explicit

A deprecated symbol is not automatically relevant. The current version must be below the recorded change boundary and the target version must reach or cross it.

### Confidence is not permission

Confidence helps prioritize findings. The `auto_fix` field controls mutation authority. A high-confidence match can still require manual review when the replacement changes call structure.

### Analysis does not execute the target project

The scanner parses source and inspects syntax trees. It does not import or run the analyzed repository. This keeps scans deterministic and avoids triggering project side effects.

## Known limitations

- The catalog is small and manually reviewed
- Cross-file type and data flow inference are not implemented
- The reverse call graph covers direct local function names
- Method receiver inference is deliberately conservative
- The browser detector is less precise than the Python AST engine
- Safe rewrites operate at line granularity
- Python syntax validation does not prove runtime compatibility

## Provenance and claims

This repository contains an independent implementation and original fixtures.

It does not include third-party papers, research datasets, benchmark traces, source archives, or copied project assets. The checked-in metrics are produced only from fixtures in this repository. The project does not claim reproduction or authorship of external results.

API migration facts are linked to the official upstream documentation embedded in each catalog rule. The rule catalog is engineering metadata, not a claim of ownership over the underlying libraries or their release notes.

## Contributing

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) before proposing a new rule. Every automatic rule needs a version boundary, a positive fixture, a negative fixture, an idempotence test, and an upstream documentation link.

## Security

ChangePilot does not execute scanned source code. Report security issues through the process in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## License

ChangePilot is available under the [MIT License](LICENSE).

documents.title: changepilot — docs/architecture.md
documents.content:
# Architecture

ChangePilot separates evidence collection, mutation, and verification. This keeps the automatic patch surface small and makes failures easier to audit.

## Inputs

The Python engine accepts:

- A Python file or project path
- Current dependency versions
- Target dependency versions
- A reviewed API change catalog

The scanner does not infer installed versions from the active environment. Callers provide the version pair explicitly so an analysis run remains reproducible.

## Version path resolver

Each `ApiChange` record defines one upgrade boundary.

```text
library
from_version
to_version
symbol
replacement
kind
risk
confidence
auto_fix
documentation_url
match_name
```

A rule is selected when the current version is below `to_version` and the requested target version reaches or crosses `to_version`.

This is a boundary model rather than a complete dependency solver. Pre-release ordering and nonstandard version schemes are outside the current scope.

## AST index

`ProjectIndex` collects:

- Import aliases
- Classes derived from Pydantic `BaseModel`
- Typed local names
- Variables created by known pandas constructors
- Function definitions
- Direct calls between local functions

`FindingVisitor` then evaluates only the rules selected for the requested version path.

Receiver checks are conservative. An untyped object with a method named `dict` is not assumed to be a Pydantic model.

## Impact tracing

The analyzer stores local call edges as `caller -> callee` and reverses them for impact traversal. Each finding starts at its enclosing function. Breadth-first search follows reverse callers for at most three hops.

This graph estimates review scope. It is not a whole-program call graph and does not resolve dynamic dispatch, imports across modules, decorators, or reflection.

## Mutation boundary

Only rules with `auto_fix=True` enter the patch set. The first release supports deterministic method and attribute renames.

Manual rules remain visible in analysis results but do not alter source. This is important for replacements such as `DataFrame.append` to `pandas.concat`, where argument shape and surrounding expressions affect the correct edit.

## Patch verification

`verify_patch` computes changed line numbers and evaluates four checks:

1. The source parses after migration
2. Safe findings no longer appear
3. Every changed line was authorized by a safe finding
4. Manual finding lines were preserved

The contract fails closed. A valid Python patch still fails when it includes an unrelated edit.

## State verification

The entity-state evaluator accepts mappings of entity names to records. It computes:

- Added records
- Deleted records
- Updated records and changed fields

Assertions match a diff type, entity, field values, and expected count. A run fails when an expected assertion is missing or when any state change remains unexplained.

This layer is independent of source migration. It can be used by a future sandbox runner to evaluate observable outcomes without requiring one exact action trace.

## Web workbench

The hosted application mirrors the same workflow with a smaller browser-safe detector:

1. Parse current and target lock text
2. Select crossed rules
3. Match source lines
4. Trace simple reverse calls
5. Stage safe replacements
6. Verify the line-level patch contract

The interface labels this boundary directly. The Python AST engine remains the reference implementation.

## Extension points

The next useful extensions are:

- Cross-file symbol indexing
- A PEP 440 version parser
- CST-based edits that preserve formatting
- Test command orchestration in disposable containers
- Learned ranking for review order
- Calibration sets for confidence scores

Each extension should preserve the current separation between proposal authority and mutation authority.
